questions.question: Which workload most strongly favors a relational database transaction?
options: A payment ledger that must update an order and payment record together
A disposable image cache
A lookup of one session by its known ID
A static file archive
questions.explanation: A relational transaction and constraints are a strong fit when related records must preserve a business invariant together.

questions.question: A service receives 9,000 peak requests per second and 92% are reads. About how many requests per second are writes before retries and background work?
questions.explanation: Writes are the remaining 8% of the workload: 9,000 multiplied by 0.08 equals 720 writes per second.

questions.question: What is the main trade-off of adding an index to support a frequent query?
options: It reduces reads for that query but adds storage and write-maintenance work
It makes every replica immediately consistent
It removes the need for a transaction
It stores a complete backup automatically
questions.explanation: Indexes provide alternate access paths, but the database must update them when indexed data changes. They should be justified by real query shapes and plans.

questions.question: Why can a read replica be the wrong place to confirm a newly completed payment?
options: Replicas cannot answer any reads
Replication lag can make the committed write temporarily invisible
Replicas automatically delete payment rows
A replica cannot have indexes
questions.explanation: Replication takes time. Route a read-after-write confirmation to the primary, or explicitly design a wait-for-freshness behavior.

questions.question: A client times out after submitting an order and does not know whether the database committed it. What is the safest next action?
options: Retry blindly until a new order appears
Look up the idempotency key or order status before retrying safely
Immediately delete the customer's cart
Read from a lagging replica and assume the result is final
questions.explanation: A timeout creates an unknown outcome. An idempotency key lets the system find or safely repeat the original intent without creating a duplicate order or charge.

questions.question: Which statement correctly separates replication from backups?
options: A replica is an independent historical backup
Backups automatically route read traffic
Replication can improve read capacity and failover, while tested backups recover from corruption or accidental deletion
Neither replication nor backups affect recovery planning
questions.explanation: Replication can copy an accidental delete or corrupt write. Independent backups and restore tests are needed to recover historical data.
